title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 51
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Telling One Person from Another
passages.text:
A. Identifying a person reliably is a problem that only appears when strangers must be distinguished at scale. In a settlement where everyone is known by sight, identification requires no technology; in a city, an army, a prison system or a border, it requires a method that works between people who have never met, and the search for such a method produced several failures before it produced anything usable.

B. The first systematic attempt measured the body. A set of careful measurements — the length of a forearm, the width of a head, the length of a particular finger — was recorded on a card and filed in a system that allowed retrieval, on the reasoning that the combination would be unique even if no single measurement was. It worked well enough to be adopted widely, and its weaknesses were practical: measurements had to be taken identically by different people in different places, and they changed as a body aged.

C. Ridge patterns on the fingers had advantages that were obvious once the comparison was made. They can be recorded without special equipment, they do not change with age, they are left behind unintentionally on surfaces, and classifying them into types allows a collection to be searched. The last property mattered as much as the uniqueness: a characteristic that cannot be filed and retrieved is of no use in identifying an unknown person.

D. The claim that has proved most difficult is not that patterns are unique but that examiners can match them reliably. Comparison of a clear recorded print with another clear recorded print is a straightforward task; comparison of a partial, smudged mark from a surface with a database of prints is a judgement made by a person, and studies in which examiners were given the same marks on separate occasions have found disagreement, including with their own earlier conclusions.

E. Contextual information has been shown to affect those judgements in ways examiners do not intend. Where an examiner knows that a suspect has confessed, or that other evidence points a particular way, the rate at which a match is declared changes, and this holds for conscientious professionals working carefully. The response adopted in better laboratories is to withhold irrelevant case information from the person doing the comparison rather than to ask them to ignore it.

F. What the field is moving towards is a change in how conclusions are expressed. Stating that two marks came from the same finger, with certainty, claims more than the method supports; stating how much more likely the evidence is under one explanation than another describes what was actually found. Courts have absorbed this slowly, because a probability is harder to act on than a certainty, and because the certainty was more useful to whoever was relying on it.

passages.title: The Material That Grew
passages.text:
Wood is the only major structural material that is manufactured by the object it is taken from, and its properties follow from having been alive rather than from any design. It is a bundle of hollow fibres running the length of the trunk, which makes it far stronger along the grain than across it, and this single fact governs everything about how it must be cut, joined and loaded. A material with different strength in different directions is more difficult to use and more efficient when used correctly.

Water is the complication in every application. Wood is full of it when cut, loses it to the surrounding air, shrinks as it does so, and continues to exchange moisture with its surroundings for as long as it exists — swelling in humid conditions and shrinking in dry ones, and doing so unevenly because it shrinks more across the grain than along it. Seasoning is the controlled removal of that water, and almost every defect in a wooden object can be traced to it having been done badly or not at all.

The variability is what industrial users find hardest. Two boards from the same tree differ, knots interrupt the fibres and concentrate stress, and grain direction wanders, so a designer cannot assume the strength of a given piece with the confidence that steel permits. Engineered products address this directly: cutting timber into small pieces, discarding defects and bonding the remainder produces a material with predictable properties made from unpredictable input.

Those engineered products have changed what can be built. Panels and beams made from bonded layers can be manufactured in large sizes, carry loads in more than one direction, and are strong enough for buildings of a height that timber could not previously reach, while weighing considerably less than concrete equivalents. The constraint has moved from strength to the questions that arise when a structural material is combustible, which are addressed by mass rather than by treatment.

Fire behaviour is better than the intuition suggests and worse than its advocates sometimes claim. A heavy timber member burns on the outside and forms a layer of char that insulates the wood beneath, so it loses strength predictably and slowly rather than suddenly, which is a genuine advantage over unprotected steel. This applies to large sections and not to light frames, and the difference between the two is the difference between a controlled outcome and a rapid one.

The carbon argument is real and routinely stated too simply. A tree removes carbon while growing and a wooden building stores it for as long as the building stands, which is a genuine benefit; whether the whole system removes carbon depends on what happens to the forest afterwards, how the wood is disposed of eventually, and what material would have been used instead. The accounting is favourable in most realistic cases and it is an accounting exercise, not a property of the material.

passages.title: Paying the Doctor
passages.text:
How a health system pays for care determines what care it gets, and this is more predictable than most policy relationships. Every payment method creates an incentive, none is neutral, and the failures of each are visible in systems that use it — which means the choice is not between a distorted arrangement and an undistorted one but between distortions, chosen with an understanding of which are tolerable.

Paying for each item of service rewards volume directly. A clinician paid per procedure has a financial interest in performing more of them, and the observed consequence in systems built this way is high rates of tests, imaging and interventions whose benefit to the patient is marginal, alongside good availability and short waits. The overtreatment is not fraud; it operates through genuine clinical uncertainty resolved consistently in the direction that also pays.

Paying a fixed sum per registered patient reverses the incentive precisely. A practice receiving a set amount per person on its list has an interest in that person needing little, which encourages prevention and continuity and also rewards doing less, including less that was needed. Systems using this method show good preventive care and a persistent risk of under-provision, and they need mechanisms to detect it that the payment method does not supply.

Paying for episodes of care attempts to sit between the two. A single payment covering everything associated with a procedure — the operation, the stay, the complications, the readmission — makes the provider bear the cost of things going wrong, which aligns the incentive with getting it right first time. The difficulty is defining the boundary of an episode and adjusting for how ill the patient was, and where the adjustment is imperfect the incentive becomes one to avoid difficult patients.

Paying for measured outcomes is the arrangement most attractive in principle and hardest in practice. Outcomes depend heavily on factors outside the provider's control, particularly the patient's other conditions and circumstances, so any scheme must adjust for these; the adjustment is never complete, and providers serving the sickest and poorest populations are penalised by the residual. Several such schemes have been withdrawn after producing exactly that effect.

What systems actually do is combine methods, and the reason is now well understood. A base payment per patient with additional payments for specified activities, adjustments for complexity and a small element tied to outcomes produces a set of incentives that partly offset one another, which is less elegant than any single method and works better than all of them. Designing for the failure modes rather than for the ideal case is the recurring lesson.
